title: Maharashtra Private Bus Operators Vow No Diwali Fare Hike Despite Drought
excerpt: The state bus owners’ association says operators will hold fares at normal levels for the festival rush, citing drought-hit rural demand; state transport is adding extra buses instead.
body:
• Maharashtra's private bus operators say they will not raise fares for the Diwali rush this year, breaking with the usual festival-season surge.
  • The Maharashtra State Bus Owners' Association cited drought-hit rural demand: families in dry districts cannot absorb a hike, its president Prakash Lad said.
  • State transport is adding capacity instead — MSRTC is running 776 extra buses for the Diwali rush in the Thane division alone.
  • State rules allow private operators a capped seasonal increase of up to 30% on state-transport-linked fares; this year, operators are choosing not to use it.

Private bus operators in Maharashtra have decided not to raise fares for the Diwali travel rush, the Maharashtra State Bus Owners' Association (MSBOA) said, in a break from the seasonal surge that usually greets festival travellers. The Times of India reported the decision was driven by drought: with rural Maharashtra short of water and farm incomes squeezed, operators judged that their core passengers simply could not pay more.

"We will not burden passengers this Diwali," MSBOA president Prakash Lad said in the report, pointing to the drought conditions across the state's rural districts. The association's members run the long-distance private services that carry migrant workers and students from Mumbai, Pune and Thane back to hometowns in Marathwada, Vidarbha and the Konkan for the festival — exactly the districts where the drought has bitten hardest.

The Hike That Didn't Happen

Festival fare surges are normally built into the business. State rules let private operators charge a capped seasonal premium — up to 30% above state-transport-linked base fares on notified routes, The Times of India has reported in explaining the framework — and Diwali is the week operators count on. Waiving it is a real cost, taken, the association says, because a priced-out passenger in a drought year is a passenger lost to the season entirely.

The public system is adding supply at the same time. The Maharashtra State Road Transport Corporation is running 776 extra buses for the Diwali rush in the Thane division alone, The Hindu BusinessLine reported, part of the state carrier's annual festival deployment on its busiest corridors.

The scale of the drought explains the decision. Maharashtra has declared drought in 305 talukas this year and promised farmers ₹5,000 in relief before Diwali — the same households whose sons and daughters fill the Diwali buses home.

What Travellers Should Do

For anyone travelling within Maharashtra this Diwali: private fares should sit at normal levels, so a quote far above the usual route price is worth challenging with the operator — and the MSRTC's extra services give a state-run fallback on the busiest routes. Book early anyway; a fare freeze does not add seats, and the Diwali rush out of Mumbai and Pune fills buses days ahead regardless of price.

The bigger story sits behind the timetable. A drought severe enough to change festival pricing in India's richest state is a reminder of what this Diwali looks like away from the metros: the same week that cracker prices are jumping 30–50% in city markets, the families travelling home to dry districts are the ones operators decided not to charge more.
